findings.title: Second `self.downsize` silently replaces the width/height variant
findings.body:
Ruby has no method overloading. The new `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 overwrites the `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` defined just above it at line 145, so the 4-dimension version is dead code.

Any existing caller that passes width and height separately now breaks:
- `downsize(path, path, max, max, allow_animation: x)` raises `ArgumentError` (5 args for 3..4).
- `downsize(path, path, w, h)` binds `h` to `opts`, and `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer raises `TypeError`.

This includes the existing avatar-downsizing path and any specs that call it. Give the percentage variant a distinct name (e.g. `downsize_by`), or build the dimension string at the call site and keep a single signature.

findings.title: Animated GIF downsizing passes a percentage to gifsicle `--resize-fit`, which only accepts WxH
findings.body:
When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled and the upload is a `.gif`, `optimize` dispatches to `downsize_instructions_animated`. That reuses `resize_instructions_animated` and emits `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`.

`--resize-fit` expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage (percent scaling would be `--scale 0.8`). The command exits non-zero, `convert_with` returns false, and the return value is ignored. The loop runs 5 no-op attempts and the oversized GIF is still rejected by the size validation.

The feature does not work for animated GIFs, and each such upload wastes 5 failed process spawns.

findings.title: Loop condition and recorded filesize use `tempfile.size`, which reads a stale file descriptor after ImageOptim replaces the file
findings.body:
`Tempfile#size` on an open tempfile does `fstat` on its file descriptor, not on the path. `convert_with` runs `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!(to)`, and image_optim writes to a separate temp file and `rename`s it over the path. After the first iteration the path points to a new inode while `tempfile`'s descriptor still refers to the old, unlinked one.

So `tempfile.size` reports the size of the first `convert` output for every later iteration. Consequences:
- If that size is still above the limit, the loop always runs all 5 attempts and over-shrinks the image (about 0.8^5 linear) even after the real file is small enough.
- The stale size is passed as `filesize` to `Upload.create_for`, so a successfully shrunk image can still fail the max-size validation, or be stored with a wrong filesize.

Use `File.size(tempfile.path)` for both the loop check and the filesize argument, and make sure downstream code reads from the path rather than the old descriptor.

findings.title: Client-side size check hardcoded to 10MB for attachments too, ignoring `max_attachment_size_kb`
findings.body:
`validateUploadedFile` previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which handles both images and attachments. It now uses a hardcoded 10MB for every type, even though the server only auto-downsizes images.

- If an admin set `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10MB, users can no longer upload attachments they are allowed to upload; the client rejects them with a misleading "max 10240 KB" message.
- If the setting is below 10MB, the client no longer catches oversized attachments early. The full file is uploaded only to be rejected by the server.

The 413 handler at line 246 likewise reports a fixed 10MB that has no relation to the web server's actual limit. Keep the setting-based limit for attachments (and for images when downsizing is disabled) and only relax it for images.

findings.title: Oversized animated GIFs are silently flattened to a single frame when animated thumbnails are disabled
findings.body:
When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is false, `downsize_instructions` runs `convert #{from}[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame and writes it back over the uploaded file.

Previously an oversized animated GIF got a clear "file too large" error. Now it is silently stored as a static image. Users lose their animation with no indication of why.

Consider skipping auto-downsizing for animated images that cannot be resized with animation preserved, and returning the size error instead.

findings.title: Up to 5 ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes on a 10MB image run inside the web process
findings.body:
The new loop runs `convert` followed by a full ImageOptim pass up to 5 times on images of up to 10MB, all inside the request handling path. For API uploads with `synchronous` it runs in the request itself; otherwise it runs in `Scheduler::Defer`, a single in-process background thread shared with other deferred work.

Each iteration can take seconds of CPU on large photos, which delays all other deferred tasks in that worker. Several problems compound this:
- The `convert` exit status is ignored, so a failing conversion still costs 5 iterations.
- ImageOptim runs on every intermediate result rather than once at the end.
- The scale factor is fixed at 80% instead of being derived from the size ratio.

findings.title: No tests for auto-downsizing or the changed `OptimizedImage` API
findings.body:
The PR changes the signature and behaviour of `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` and removes `OptimizedImage.dimensions`. It also adds a new size-reduction path in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but no specs are added or updated.

A test that calls the existing 4-argument `downsize` would have exposed the method-redefinition bug. A controller spec that uploads an image above `max_image_size_kb` would exercise the loop and filesize handling, including the stale `tempfile.size` issue.
